learn.title: Purpose, mission, objectives and performance criteria

sections.heading: From purpose to targets
sections.body: A business purpose is its underlying reason for existing and the value it seeks to create. Its mission communicates a broad direction or identity. Objectives then turn that broad direction into intended results, such as profit, growth, survival or stronger cash generation. A measure, often called a KPI, is the metric used to observe progress. A target sets the desired level or deadline for that measure. The chain is: purpose → strategic priorities → objectives → measures and targets → decisions and behaviour → outcomes. Businesses may pursue several objectives at once, so managers need to decide which priorities matter most when resources are limited.

sections.heading: Keep the terms distinct
sections.body: Purpose answers “why does this organisation exist?”. A mission statement gives a broad, long-term statement of what it is for or stands for. An objective is a specific result it seeks. Profit, growth, survival and cash flow can all be objectives, but they are different: profit is the financial surplus from trading; growth means increasing the scale of the business; survival focuses on continuing to operate; and cash flow focuses on having sufficient cash available to meet commitments. A KPI is not an objective: it is a measure used to track performance. A target is the required level or deadline attached to a measure.

sections.heading: Mission, stakeholders and changing priorities
sections.body: Mission is influenced by ownership and what owners value, founders’ values, stakeholder expectations, business stage, financial position and external pressures such as competition, technology, law and social attitudes. A shareholder-owned business may emphasise financial return, while a social enterprise may give greater weight to community or environmental outcomes. Social and ethical objectives include reducing environmental impact, fair treatment of employees and suppliers, ethical sourcing and community support. These can strengthen reputation and loyalty, but may raise costs or limit short-run profit. Mission usually changes gradually, but a new owner, crisis or move into a new market can prompt a rewrite. Objectives should remain consistent with the mission, even when stakeholder demands create trade-offs.

sections.heading: Mission translated into action
sections.body: Example: A café’s mission is to provide affordable healthy food. It sets objectives to keep average prices below £5 and increase sales of healthy lines by 15% within one year. Average selling price and healthy-line sales are measures; “below £5” and “15% within one year” are targets. Non-example: saying “revenue” is an objective gives no direction about whether the business wants revenue growth, a revenue level, a timeframe or an acceptable profit position. Another non-example is treating a KPI dashboard as a strategy: measures monitor performance but do not themselves explain what the business is trying to achieve.

sections.heading: A number can improve while performance worsens
sections.body: Misconception: “A KPI is an objective.” Correction: a KPI measures progress, whereas an objective is the result sought. Misconception: “A SMART objective must be a good objective.” Correction: SMART can make an objective precise, but cannot show whether it fits the mission or creates harmful incentives. For example, a service business may target shorter call times. Staff could rush customers to hit the target, reducing first-contact resolution and harming the underlying aim of good customer service. Use a balanced set of reliable measures, including non-financial leading indicators where useful, and check for unintended behavioural effects.

sections.heading: Check alignment and trade-offs
sections.body: A business says its purpose is reliable service and its mission stresses long-term customer relationships. Explain: (1) which two objectives it might choose; (2) one financial and one non-financial measure it could use; (3) how a target based only on speed could distort employee behaviour; and (4) why its mission might change if a new owner prioritised environmental impact. In your explanation, distinguish the desired outcome from the number used to monitor it.

key_terms.definition: The underlying reason an organisation exists and the value it intends to create.
A broad statement of a business’s direction, intended role or identity.
A result that a business aims to achieve.
An aim to generate a financial surplus from trading.
An aim to increase the scale of the business.
An aim to continue operating, often especially important in difficult conditions.
An aim to maintain sufficient cash available to meet payments when due.
A metric used to observe performance and progress.
A desired level or deadline attached to a measure.
Goals beyond financial return, such as reducing environmental impact or treating employees and suppliers fairly.
A person or group affected by, or able to affect, a business.

items.prompt: State the difference between a business’s purpose and its mission statement.
items.answer: Purpose is why the business exists; a mission statement communicates its broad direction or intended role.
items.explanation: Purpose is the underlying reason for existence, while mission is the broad statement used to express that direction.

items.prompt: Classify each as an objective, measure or target: (a) improve cash flow, (b) monthly cash balance, (c) maintain a monthly cash balance of at least £30,000 by September.
items.explanation: The objective is the result sought, the measure observes cash performance, and the target adds a required level and deadline.

items.prompt: Explain one difference between a survival objective and a growth objective, and justify why survival may take priority for a business facing a cash crisis.
items.answer: Survival aims to keep the business operating, whereas growth aims to increase its scale. Survival may take priority because the business cannot pursue growth if it cannot meet payments and continues to trade only for a short time.
items.explanation: The objectives have different time horizons and priorities. Immediate financial pressure can make continued operation more important than expansion.

items.prompt: A UK clothing retailer has a mission centred on responsible fashion. Give one social or ethical objective and one measure that would fit this mission.
items.answer: Objective: improve fair treatment of suppliers. Measure: the proportion of suppliers assessed against the retailer’s supplier standards.
items.explanation: The objective reflects responsible fashion, while the proportion assessed is a measurable indicator of progress. Other suitably aligned social or ethical objectives and measures are valid.

items.prompt: A profitable family-owned food producer is bought by a social enterprise that places high value on reducing environmental impact. Judge whether the producer should revise its mission immediately.
items.answer: A revision is likely to be justified because ownership and owner values strongly influence mission. However, the business should ensure the revised mission remains realistic given its financial position and can be translated into achievable objectives.
items.explanation: A change of owner can prompt a mission rewrite. The judgement is not automatic because mission must still be strategically feasible and aligned with the business’s circumstances.

items.prompt: A manager says: “Our KPI is to answer every call within 20 seconds, so excellent customer service is guaranteed.” What is wrong with this claim?
items.answer: Answering speed is a measure and target, not proof of excellent service. Staff may rush calls, reducing resolution or customer understanding.
items.explanation: A single measure can distort behaviour. The underlying objective needs other relevant measures, such as first-contact resolution, as well as attention to the customer outcome.

items.prompt: A delivery firm exists to make local shopping more convenient. Its mission promises dependable, lower-impact deliveries. Select the best set of aligned objectives: A. maximise number of deliveries per driver, regardless of complaints; B. improve reliability, protect cash availability and reduce environmental impact; C. publish a KPI dashboard with no stated results; D. cut delivery quality to raise short-run profit.
items.answer: B. Improve reliability, protect cash availability and reduce environmental impact.
items.explanation: Option B turns the purpose and mission into compatible operational, financial and ethical objectives. A and D risk misalignment, while C gives measures without objectives.
